title: "Did Canada's 2024 Tariff on Chinese Steel Change Where Canada Buys Its Steel?"
author: "Xiang Zheng, University of Toronto"
date: "October 2026"
output:
  pdf_document:
    fig_width: 6.5
    fig_height: 2.0
geometry: margin=0.75in

---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

read_cimt <- function(file, country_name) {
  read_csv(file, skip = 1, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    filter(str_detect(Period, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")) |>
    mutate(country = country_name)
}

imports <- map2_dfr(c("total.csv", "china.csv"), c("World", "China"), read_cimt) |>
  rename(value = `Value ($)`) |>
  mutate(month = as.Date(Period), hs6 = str_sub(Commodity, 1, 7))

covered_hs6 <- c(
  "7206.10","7206.90","7207.11","7207.12","7207.19","7207.20","7208.10","7208.25",
  "7208.26","7208.27","7208.36","7208.37","7208.38","7208.39","7208.40","7208.51",
  "7208.52","7208.53","7208.54","7208.90","7209.15","7209.16","7209.17","7209.18",
  "7209.25","7209.26","7209.27","7209.28","7209.90","7210.11","7210.12","7210.20",
  "7210.30","7210.41","7210.49","7210.50","7210.61","7210.69","7210.70","7210.90",
  "7211.13","7211.14","7211.19","7211.23","7211.29","7211.90","7212.10","7212.20",
  "7212.30","7212.40","7212.50","7212.60","7213.10","7213.20","7213.91","7213.99",
  "7214.20","7214.30","7214.91","7214.99","7215.10","7215.50","7215.90","7216.10",
  "7216.21","7216.22","7216.31","7216.32","7216.33","7216.40","7216.50","7216.99",
  "7217.10","7217.20","7217.30","7217.90","7218.10","7218.91","7218.99","7219.11",
  "7219.12","7219.13","7219.14","7219.21","7219.22","7219.23","7219.24","7219.31",
  "7219.32","7219.33","7219.34","7219.35","7219.90","7220.12","7220.20","7220.90",
  "7221.00","7222.11","7222.19","7222.20","7222.30","7222.40","7223.00","7224.10",
  "7224.90","7225.11","7225.19","7225.30","7225.40","7225.50","7225.91","7225.92",
  "7225.99","7226.11","7226.19","7226.20","7226.91","7226.92","7226.99","7227.10",
  "7227.20","7227.90","7228.20","7228.30","7228.40","7228.50","7228.60","7228.70",
  "7229.20","7229.90"
)

# China's overall share, before vs surtax-only period
overall <- imports |>
  group_by(country, month) |>
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(share = China / World)

pre_share  <- mean(overall$share[overall$month <= as.Date("2024-07-01")])
post_share <- mean(overall$share[overall$month >= as.Date("2024-11-01") &
                                 overall$month <= as.Date("2025-02-01")])

# Difference-in-differences data
did_data <- imports |>
  mutate(group = if_else(hs6 %in% covered_hs6, "On surtax list", "Not on list")) |>
  group_by(country, group, month) |>
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(china_share = China / World)

did_reg <- did_data |>
  filter(!(month >= as.Date("2024-08-01") & month <= as.Date("2024-10-01"))) |>
  mutate(covered = as.integer(group == "On surtax list"),
         post    = as.integer(month >= as.Date("2024-11-01")),
         month_f = factor(month))

# DiD estimate = change in the monthly gap (listed minus unlisted) after the surtax,
# with Newey-West standard errors (3 lags) to allow for correlation between months
did_diff <- did_reg |>
  select(month, post, group, china_share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = china_share) |>
  mutate(diff = `On surtax list` - `Not on list`) |>
  arrange(month)

did_fit <- function(end) {
  m  <- lm(diff ~ post, data = filter(did_diff, month <= as.Date(end)))
  V  <- NeweyWest(m, lag = 3, prewhite = FALSE)
  ci <- coefci(m, vcov. = V)
  c(est = unname(coef(m)["post"]),
    lo  = ci["post", 1],
    hi  = ci["post", 2],
    p   = coeftest(m, vcov = V)["post", 4])
}
main <- did_fit("2025-02-01")
long <- did_fit("2025-06-01")

pp  <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "p < 0.001", paste0("p = ", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
```

**The question.** In October 2024, Canada added a 25% tax on steel from China. When one
supplier becomes more expensive, buyers tend to switch to others. Did China's share of
Canada's steel imports fall, and was the tax the reason, rather than seasons, price changes,
long-term trends or the trade dispute with the United States that began in 2025?

**What I did.** I used Statistics Canada's monthly import records for 167 types of steel
products from January 2023 to August 2026. The tax covered 130 of these products and not
the other 37. The key test compares how China's share changed for taxed products with how
it changed for untaxed products over the same months: if the tax was responsible, the drop
should show up mainly in the taxed group. I also compared the same season one year apart,
measured imports by weight as well as value, and checked whether the two groups were
already moving apart before the tax.

```{r did-plot}
did_data |>
  filter(month <= as.Date("2025-06-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = china_share, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date(c("2024-08-26", "2024-10-22")), linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2024-08-20"), y = Inf, label = "Tax announced",
           angle = 90, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.4, size = 2.8) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2024-10-16"), y = Inf, label = "Tax starts",
           angle = 90, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.4, size = 2.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c("Not on list" = "Untaxed products", "On surtax list" = "Taxed products")) +
  labs(title = "China's share of Canada's steel imports: taxed vs. untaxed products",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of import value", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**What I found.**

- **China's share fell.** It dropped from `r pct(pre_share)` before the tax to
  `r pct(post_share)` in the four months after it started. The drop also shows up by weight and
  remains when comparing the same winter months a year apart. Imports from China themselves fell by about 39%
  compared with the same winter a year earlier.
- **The drop was mainly in taxed products.** Before the tax, China's shares in the two
  groups moved together. Afterwards, its share of taxed products fell to about 2-3%, while
  its share of untaxed products returned to its usual range.
- **The size of the effect: about 2 percentage points.** China's share of taxed products
  fell by about `r pp(-main["est"])` points more than its share of untaxed products,
  roughly a third of its earlier share. Including months up to June 2025 gives a larger
  drop of about `r pp(-long["est"])` points, but that period overlaps with the U.S. dispute.
- **Who gained.** Comparing taxed and untaxed products for each supplier, Japan is the most
  likely gainer, though the evidence is not conclusive. For the United States and smaller
  suppliers, the data are too noisy to tell.

**How sure can we be?** Only four months separate the tax from the 2025 trade dispute, so
the clearest result rests on very little data. Depending on how the uncertainty is
measured, it falls just on one side or the other of the usual line for statistical
significance, and in a comparison that keeps the 167 products separate its likely range
includes zero. The evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. A smaller Chinese share
also does not by itself show that the tax was good for Canada.

*Full report and R code: https://github.com/betterandy24/canada-steel-surtax*
